Mawkish

MAW-kish · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Mawkish is sentimental in a feeble, cloying, or insincere way.

Critics panned the film's ending as mawkish, calling the tearful reunion scene forced and overly sweet.

Worked Example

The greeting card's mawkish verse, dripping with forced rhymes about eternal love, made her roll her eyes and put it back on the shelf.

Mawkish sentimentality feels manufactured or excessive, like emotion poured on too thick to feel genuine.

How Mawkish Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

cloying

cloying: excessively sweet or sentimental, to an unpleasant degree

treacly

treacly: excessively and stickily sweet or sentimental

Antonyms

restrained

restrained: controlled, not showing strong emotion

understated

understated: presented in a subtle or low-key way

How Strong Is It? — tender → nauseating → mawkish

tender vs. mawkish

tender vs. mawkish: A tender moment just shows real warmth, without piling anything on.

nauseating vs. mawkish

nauseating vs. mawkish: A truly nauseating tribute piles on so much forced emotion it turns the stomach, beyond ordinary mawkishness.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — mawk

root — mawk: maggot (obsolete/dialectal); by extension, something sickening (Middle English)

suffix — -ish

suffix — -ish: having the quality of (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: Mawkish traces back to the obsolete word mawk ("maggot") + -ish -- it originally described something sickly or nauseating, a sense now applied to feelings instead of food.

Use the root in a new word: queasy

Use the root in a new word: queasy: If overly sugary sentimentality makes your stomach turn, you might say it makes you feel queasy -- capturing the same sickly sense mawkish carries.

Mawkish is almost always a criticism -- it means sentimentality that feels fake, forced, or overdone, not just emotional.
